newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal stirs strong emotions among Americans.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal stirs strong emotions among Americans.

text.p: News of Friday's historic tobacco settlement stirred strong emotions among Americans, leaving some to wonder if the cigarette industry would pay enough for its role in the lives of millions of smokers.

"I think that's not enough money because people have died because of smoking," said 36-year-old Maria Arbelaz, a Miami bank worker who believes the industry has lied for decades about the ill-effects of tobacco.
Worse still has been the alleged marketing of cigarettes to youngsters, a practice which she said was not unlike "introducing drugs to children. It's so bad. They should never have done that."

Under the tentative agreement announced in Washington, the tobacco industry would pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to help states recoup tax money spent treating ill smokers. The industry also would admit to the ill-effects of smoking and accept federal regulation of their products and advertising.

The settlement drew fierce criticism from nonsmoking advocates including Norma Broin, lead plaintiff in a $5 billion tobacco lawsuit filed in Florida on behalf of 60,000 flight attendants who say they became ill after breathing secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.
Broin said in a telephone interview from her home in Stafford, Virginia, that she was "just sick" about the settlement.
"This is just so wrong," the 42-year-old nonsmoker fumed. "This is just a fabulous, fabulous deal for the tobacco companies."
Some skeptics in the general public took issue with the dollar amount of the settlement, suggesting that the figure might only look good on paper.

"$368.5 billion? Is that in today's money?" quipped a a non-smoking office worker as he hurried to his car. "It's like the lottery. $20,000 a year for 50 years adds up to a million bucks. But it's not really a million bucks."
Others said that whatever the real financial consequences of the agreement, the costs would inevitably get passed on to consumers.
"Prices will go up about 30 cents a pack now," said 25-year-old Sung Park, whose family-run Atlanta convenience sells cigarettes for $2 a pack.
Meanwhile, smokers poured scorn on the prospects for ever-tougher restrictions on cigarettes, just as non-smokers by and large greeted the news as a step in the right direction.
Nearly everyone welcomed curbs on the marketing of tobacco products to teen-agers.

"I think it's a really good thing for kids. My goal ... is to see smoking stopped in our lifetime. And it's not going to stop if Joe Camel can say 'hey, be cool. Light up," said Tom Walters, a 33-year-old non-smoker who works for a financial company in Boston.
But Tom Greenleaf, a 66-year-old San Francisco stockbroker, saw the settlement as more evidence of government interference in the lives of Americans.
"The federal government shouldn't get their fingers in everything. This is supposed to be a free enterprise society," declared Greenleaf, who started smoking at the age of 15.
Samuel Moore, a 43-year-old Texas salesman, complained that smokers were fast becoming second-class citizens and that restrictions on smoking in public places were unfair.

"When I started about 25 years ago, everybody smoked and there was no trouble. But now you are not allowed anywhere. It has gone too far the other way," he said, while taking a puff outside his office building in Dallas.
In New York City, which boasts some of the most stringent nonsmoking rules in the country, the reception was far more accomodating.

"It's great. Personally, I think they should ban tobacco period. I've known too many people who've died of cancer because of smoking. I'd like to see them get as much money as they can out of (the tobacco companies)," said Rose Wigutow, 66, a Huntington, New York, housewife.
Even some smokers grudgingly accepted the settlement's penalties.

"I think it's probably a positive thing, but I think the government should be concerned with other things, more important things," 25-year-old Pamela Yee said in Boston. "As adults, we're aware of the dangers of smoking and we're chosing to smoke," she added.
